name: Collaborative playlists: everyone adds a song
object: Collaborative playlists, the Spotify feature that lets a listener invite friends to add their own songs to a shared playlist
audience: friend groups planning a shared moment together, like a road trip or a festival weekend
message: This video tells friend groups that turning a solo playlist into a group one just takes naming it, inviting friends, and letting everyone drop in their own songs.

moments.what: A woman lies relaxed on her bed scrolling her phone, hand-drawn stars popping in around her, while bold lettering over the shot pitches building a playlist together with friends.
moments.copy: Make a playlist with your friends.

moments.what: Cut to the actual app: a 'name your playlist' modal with a keyboard open, a road-trip themed name being typed in, and a Create button below it.

Quick cuts of a guy pushing his sunglasses up in a car and a woman jumping down some steps outside, both shots stamped with bold lettering about pulling friends into the playlist, doodled hearts and flames flying around them.

Back to the app: a shared playlist named 'Festival' with several friends listed as collaborators and a scrollable queue of songs they've each added, while a woman on her bed smiles at her phone and lettering states the payoff.
moments.copy: Everyone adds their own songs to the same playlist.

moments.what: The screen bursts into bright pop-art starburst graphics in quick cuts, then cuts to black and settles on the plain Spotify wordmark and logo.

cta: No spoken or typed 'try it now' line; the video simply demonstrates the three steps (name it, add friends, add songs) and then closes on the Spotify logo once the shared playlist is built.
why: Splitting the pitch into three short, literally-labelled beats (make it, add friends, add songs) makes a feature that could be abstract feel like a checklist anyone could repeat in under a minute, and cutting straight to real app screens after each label proves each step actually exists rather than just claiming it. The all-text, no-narration treatment and rapid vertical cuts match how the feature itself gets used and shared.
